catalog_quote: PHONOLOGICAL WORDS. Phonological words in Sedang are either mono- or bisyllabic. Monosyllabic words consist of one (usually) stressed "main syllable". Bisyllabic words consist of a preliminary unstressed "presyllable" and a (following) stressed main syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2 'StressTyp2') records Sedang as final-stressed (final stress). Smith's statement that stress falls on the main syllable, which follows the unstressed presyllable, is exactly final stress in the mono-/sesquisyllabic word; it refines the record by giving the domain (presyllable + main syllable, maximally two syllables in native words), the phonetic basis (presyllable vowel always schwa, unstressed), and the observation that many monosyllabic function words are unstressed in context. Note the copy read is the 1979 published edition of the 1975 dissertation, not the dissertation PDF listed.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (unstressed presyllable + main syllable). Stress is on the main syllable, which is always the last syllable of the word; the presyllable (always schwa) is unstressed. Stress is therefore predictable/non-contrastive; the contrastive suprasegmental is tense/lax register (voice quality), and Smith states (p. 32) that pitch does not pertain to Sedang register.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Only related remarks: the adversative prefix la- vowel 'is sometimes spoken as a phonetic [o] with slight stress, whereas the presyllable vowel is always schwa and unstressed except in intentionally slow speech' (p. 149); story-telling reduplication sets up 'a rhythm between stressed and unstressed syllables' (p. 152); poetic metre 'is alternate stressed and unstressed syllables' (p. 156).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllables are '(usually)' stressed: monosyllabic function words are stressed only in (unnatural) isolation and 'many in context are unstressed' (p. 21). One trisyllabic derivative with la- (lakade) exists; its la- vowel may carry slight stress (p. 149). Elision of stressed oh in negatives causes 'loss of a stress peak' (p. 125).
new_statements.identity_note: Smith describes the Sedang of Kontum province (Dak To / Kontum area, informants Hmou, Tua, Dih, Be), the standard/central variety; chapter 5 treats dialectal variation but the stress statement is made for Sedang generally. The 1979 book is the published edition of the 1975 UPenn dissertation (Acknowledgements p. iii); the listed SIL dissertation PDF (item 12352) is a dead link (404 on both the direct PDF and the archive record).

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict, stress on the final = main syllable of a maximally bisyllabic presyllable+main-syllable word) rests on a verbatim, page-confirmed statement in the standard reference grammar (Smith 1979 PL B-50, section 4.1 p. 20), which we hold as full PDF and text; the same book repeats the pattern at 4.4 (p. 46) and 12.3 (p. 149), and notes monosyllabic function words are often unstressed in context (p. 21), none of which conflicts with the classification. No better or instrumental source exists per Glottolog and Crossref; the only newer work is a 2014 Brill handbook sketch by the same author with Sidwell (paywalled), unlikely to change anything. The record's top-level quote/cite/grade fields are blank while the verbatim primary quotation sits in 'sources'/'the domain quotation', so the only action suggested is to populate the strength of the evidence as primary-source-verified; no reclassification.
